Make, n8n or a custom API: choosing an AI workflow platform

Deployment · control · cost structure · operations · lock-in

The problem: to wire LLMs into business processes, should you pick a visual platform (Make), a self-hostable open-source tool (n8n), or write your own integration? The short answer: all three call the same model APIs at the same prices — the difference is not "AI cost" but deployment shape, data boundary, platform fees and operational responsibility. This article gives a decision framework and declares no product the winner.

1. What the three options are

· Make (cloud iPaaS): a fully managed visual platform where a Scenario is a trigger plus a sequence of modules; it offers a REST-style open API and a custom-app mechanism, and most administrative endpoints require a paid subscription (see the Make developer documentation, verified 2026-10-28);
· n8n (fair-code automation tool): defined in its official documentation as a "fair-code licensed workflow automation tool"; you can install it yourself (the documentation lists Docker Compose and other deployment options) or use its cloud service (see the n8n documentation, verified 2026-10-28);
· Custom API: orchestrate model calls directly in code (queue + functions + scheduled jobs), with no platform layer — all the control and all the responsibility.

2. A six-dimension comparison framework

DimensionMake (cloud iPaaS)n8n (fair-code / self-hostable)Custom API
DeploymentFully managed SaaS, zero opsSelf-hosted (Docker etc.) or official cloudYour own environment, full control
Data residencyData flows through platform serversData stays in your network when self-hostedData stays in your network
Time to first workflowFast: visual assemblyFast: visual assemblySlow: development and debugging
Customization ceilingLimited by platform modules and APICustom code nodes possibleUnlimited
Cost structurePlatform per operation + LLM APISelf-host = server cost / cloud = subscription + LLM APIInfrastructure only + LLM API
Operational burdenBorne by the platformSelf-host: yours (upgrades, availability)Entirely yours
Vendor lock-inHigh: workflow assets live on the platformMedium: can migrate to self-hostingLow

The table deliberately compares structure, not prices; both vendors' pricing was verified and appears in the next section. LLM API costs are identical across all three — estimate them on one basis with the cost calculator.

3. Platform pricing and billing units (verified 2026-10-28)

Make (USD, page list prices): Free $0/month (explicitly including 1,000 credits/month); Core $9 / Pro $16 / Teams $29 per month (these numbers are shown in a "Save 15%" context, and the page does not state whether they are monthly or annual billing; side-by-side monthly/annual pricing is not given); Enterprise is contact-sales. When credits run out: scenarios stop running; you can upgrade, buy add-ons (only 1,000/10,000 bundles at "a fixed price defined in the subscription" — the number is not public) or enable auto-purchase of 10,000 credits on Core/Pro/Teams; credits expire each cycle and do not roll over. What a credit counts: most module actions in a scenario count as 1 credit each (read/search/create/update/transform/aggregate/iterate all count); error handlers and Router modules do not; Make Code is billed separately at 2 credits/second; the vendor says a single scenario run consumes "from 2 credits to thousands". Source: Make official pricing page (second verification 2026-10-28).

n8n (EUR, page list prices): Starter €20/month (annual, includes 2,500 workflow executions/month); Pro €50/month (annual, 10,000 executions/month); Business €667/month (annual, 40,000 executions/month, self-hosted only); Community edition is free and self-hosted (via GitHub). What an execution counts: one execution = the whole workflow completing once, regardless of how many steps or how much data it processes. Source: n8n official pricing page.

The two units are not interchangeable: one Make credit ≈ one module action, while one n8n execution = one full run (which may contain dozens of modules). Comparing "10,000 credits" with "10,000 executions" directly is wrong — the same flow can consume an order of magnitude differently on each platform. Items not published (not guessed): how many credits each Make paid tier includes, monthly billing prices and add-on bundle prices; n8n monthly billing prices, overage rates and the cloud Business launch date.

4. Three cost layers and one example workflow

Three layers: ① platform subscription/usage (Make credits or n8n cloud executions; with self-hosting, ② infrastructure — servers and ops labor); ③ LLM API fees (identical across all three — see list prices in the model library). Compute the layers separately instead of asking "which total is lowest".

Example workflow (illustrative assumptions, not measured statistics): 500 runs/day of "form → AI tagging → write to sheet", each with one model call (2,000 input / 800 output tokens, 30% cache hit rate). 15,000 runs a month:

· Make side (assuming 5 credits per run: trigger + fetch + trim + HTTP + write): 15,000 × 5 = 75,000 credits/month. Included quotas per tier are not public, so no official plan combination can be priced — the following is a model estimate (not an official quote): linear extrapolation at the publicly shown Pro unit price of $1.60 per 1,000 credits gives 75,000 × $1.60 ÷ 1,000 ≈ $120/month. Basis and limits: ① subscription-included quotas not counted (not public); ② the official path is "subscription + 1,000/10,000 add-on bundles" at non-public fixed prices, so linear extrapolation exceeds the official bundling rules; ③ the actual monthly fee must follow Make's official quote/console.
· n8n cloud route: 1 run = 1 execution → 15,000 executions/month. Pro at €50/month (annual) includes only 10K, so it is exceeded; the vendor says over-quota usage does not stop service, but Starter/Pro overage rates are listed only as "Capped" with numbers not public — the exact cloud monthly fee cannot be determined from public pages; cloud Business is not yet available (waitlist only).
· n8n self-hosting route: Business at €667/month annual (40K executions/month; the license key must connect to n8n's license server daily) + your own server and operations cost (sizing undecided, not estimated). Note €667 is a self-hosted plan price, not a cloud price — the two are not interchangeable.
· LLM API side (identical for all three): at DeepSeek V4.1 Flash off-peak rates ≈ ¥7/month (15,000 runs × ≈¥0.00046 per run; list-price estimate from models.json, verified 2026-10-28);
· How to read it: at this volume, platform/infrastructure cost (tens to hundreds of USD, with the Make side estimable only) dwarfs the API fee (single-digit CNY) — optimize "flow complexity and run count" before obsessing over model unit prices. One order of magnitude smaller, Make's free tier (1,000 credits/month) or n8n's trial may be enough outright.

Limitations (labeled item by item): 5 credits/run is an illustrative assumption (official range: 2 to thousands per run); Make's per-tier included quotas, add-on fixed prices and monthly billing prices are not public; n8n monthly billing prices and overage numbers are not public; self-hosting infrastructure is not estimated. These are worked examples from documentation research — not industry averages, not measured bills; pricing follows official sites, verified 2026-10-28.

5. Choosing by scenario (including when not to choose)

· Small team validating fast: a visual platform is quicker; prefer fully managed when business data is not sensitive (one less ops chore);
· Data must not leave the intranet: self-hosted n8n or a custom API; neither hands business data to a third-party platform;
· High volume with ops capability: self-hosting is usually cheapest overall (no per-operation fees), but rate limiting, retries, monitoring and alerting become your own job — they come built-in on platforms;
· Flows change frequently: visual tools rewire links; custom APIs need code changes plus redeployment;
· Not sure yet: trial at low volume on a platform and measure real token consumption (the architecture section of the Make workflow cost guide generalizes to all three options), then decide whether to migrate.

6. An often-overlooked fact

Model APIs are the shared raw material of all three options, priced by the vendors (the list prices in this site's models.json, each individually verifiable). What a platform decision should really compare: platform fees, operations labor, data boundary and lock-in cost — not "which option gets cheaper model calls": none does.
